I'm tracing the query `a.is_null() & ~a.is_in([1], nulls_equal=True)` through the classifier. The `is_null` part comes out as Null nullability and gets pushed to opaque. The negated `is_in([1])` goes down the IsIn branch and records `[1]` as disallowed no matter what `nulls_equal` is set to. Next I'll check `resolve_deferred`, specifically whether nullability is Null and there's a value constant.

So the disallowed set makes the whole predicate unsat, which seems wrong when nulls_equal=True, since ~is_in([1]) is true for null there. Checking the haystack-with-None and nulls_equal=False cases, those come out empty as expected. The `|` version avoids this because it goes opaque, and the negated membership alone doesn't tighten anything.

I'm checking whether the filter ordering matters, and whether chaining two filters or the optimizer's predicate pushdown merges them first. I also want to see where `has_value_constraint` is used, since `drops_nulls` treats the allowed set as non-null, but the disallowed set only implies non-null when `nulls_equal=False`.

The disallowed set is the part that's off: `classify_negation` records `[1]` as disallowed even when `nulls_equal=True`, and `has_value_constraint` then reads that as a null-dropping constraint. Restricting the disallowed recording to `nulls_equal=False`, or tracking it separately, looks like the simplest fix, since the `a == 1` fixed-value check stays valid either way.

I'm going to check whether the rule that combines filters runs before this classifier sees the predicate, and find every caller of `has_value_constraint` and `add_disallowed`. My guess is that `resolve_deferred` is the only caller of the first, and that `classify_negation` and `merge_from` are the only callers of the second. A guard in `classify_negation` that skips recording when `nulls_equal` is true looks like the minimal fix, though tracking disallowed values separately could work too.
